chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Market Cycles, Era by Era

body.text: The 1990s gave India the reforms, institutions and foreign capital that made its modern bull markets possible. They also gave Indian investors three booms and three busts in a decade, and a Sensex that was lower in 2003 than in 1992.

children.text: Lesson 3.1 ended in mid 1991, with India close to defaulting on its foreign debts. This lesson follows the next 12 years. It is the most compressed set of cycles in Indian market history: a reform euphoria wrecked by a securities scam, an IPO and foreign-money boom that left behind hundreds of vanished companies, and a technology mania that ended in another scam and a frozen mutual fund. Individual scams from this era have their own stories. The focus here is the pattern that connects them, and the lasting market infrastructure that came out of the wreckage.

children.text: In July 1991, the government of Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, used the crisis to push through reforms that had been debated for years. Industrial licensing was abolished for most industries, import duties were cut, foreign investment was welcomed, and the Controller of Capital Issues was scrapped in 1992, letting companies price their own share issues. SEBI received statutory powers in 1992, and foreign institutional investors were allowed into Indian shares from September 1992. In Kindleberger's terms from Lesson 2.1, this was a textbook displacement: a real, enormous change in what Indian companies could earn. The problem, as always, was what happened next.

markDefs.definition: Short-term deals in which banks sold government securities and agreed to buy them back later. In 1991 to 1992, weak controls allowed brokers to use these transactions to route bank money into the stock market.

let bank money flow to brokers, with the scam commonly estimated at around ₹4,000 crore. In 1999 to 2001, a cooperative bank in Gujarat, Madhavpura Mercantile Cooperative Bank, lent heavily to Ketan Parekh's operations and collapsed when prices fell. The names changed. The loop from Lesson 1.3 did not.

body.title: Sensex at major turning points, 1990 to 2003 (approximate)

body.label: A lost decade of its own
body.context: After 11 years of reforms, rising GDP and three bull markets, the index was about 36% lower. Dividends softened the damage, but investors who bought at the 1992 peak lost heavily in real terms.

body.title: Measure the Decade
body.prompt: Using the approximate figures above, the Sensex went from 4,500 to 2,900 over 11 years. What was its CAGR over that period, before dividends? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: CAGR = (2,900 ÷ 4,500) to the power 1/11, minus 1 = 0.644 to the power 0.0909, minus 1 ≈ −3.9% a year. Compare that with the 23% a year the Sensex delivered from 1979 to 1990 in Lesson 3.1. The 1992 starting point, at the top of a scam-fuelled euphoria, decided the outcome far more than India's growth did.

children.text: The IPO Flood and the Vanishing Companies

The middle cycle holds the lesson most relevant to today's investors. Once the Controller of Capital Issues was abolished, companies could set their own issue prices, and disclosure rules had not yet caught up. Between roughly 1993 and 1996, thousands of companies raised money from the public, many at inflated premiums, many with little real business. Retail investors, fresh from watching the Sensex more than double in a year, applied for almost everything. Hundreds of these companies later became untraceable, with promoters disappearing along with the money raised. The government and SEBI eventually drew up lists of vanishing companies, but most investors never recovered anything.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Why did the abolition of the Controller of Capital Issues in 1992, a genuine reform, contribute to a wave of poor-quality IPOs in the following years?
options: It banned foreign investors from applying to IPOs
It let companies set their own prices before disclosure rules, due diligence and investor scepticism had caught up, during a euphoric market
It forced all companies to list on the Calcutta Stock Exchange
It required IPOs to be priced below book value
body.explanation: Freeing issue pricing was the right long-term move, but it arrived in the euphoria stage of a cycle, before SEBI's disclosure and eligibility rules were mature. In a hot market, demand for new issues is driven by recent gains rather than the quality of the business, and weak promoters take advantage. SEBI's later rules on eligibility, disclosure and book building were largely a response.

events.title: SEBI gets statutory powers, FIIs arrive
events.description: The SEBI Act gives the regulator legal authority, the Controller of Capital Issues is abolished, and foreign institutional investors are allowed to invest in Indian shares from September.

events.title: NSE begins equity trading
events.description: The National Stock Exchange, promoted by public financial institutions, launches nationwide screen-based trading, ending the dominance of the Bombay trading ring and bringing transparent prices to investors across India. BSE moves to its own screen-based system, BOLT, in 1995.

events.title: Shares go electronic
events.description: The Depositories Act is passed and NSDL begins operations, allowing shares to be held in dematerialised form. Forged and lost certificates start to become history. The Nifty 50 index is launched the same year.

events.title: External shocks
events.description: The Asian financial crisis hits regional markets from mid 1997, and international sanctions follow India's nuclear tests in May 1998. The Sensex slides back toward the lows of the decade.

events.title: Derivatives trading begins
events.description: Index futures start trading on NSE and BSE in June 2000, with options and single-stock derivatives following in 2001.

events.title: Scandal, a frozen fund and a clean-up
events.description: The Ketan Parekh scandal breaks after the Budget in March. In July, UTI suspends repurchases in its US-64 scheme, which millions of households treated as safe, and the government steps in to protect small unitholders. SEBI ends badla, and rolling settlement is introduced for all shares.

events.title: The bottom, and a quiet turn
events.description: The Sensex bottoms near 2,900 in April. UTI is restructured. Few investors notice that corporate earnings are recovering and interest rates have fallen, the conditions for the boom covered in Lesson 3.3.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The National Stock Exchange began screen-based equity trading in the year ___.
body.explanation: NSE launched its capital market segment in November 1994. Nationwide electronic trading, followed by dematerialised shares from 1996, did more to protect ordinary investors than almost any single rule, because it made prices visible and ended bad deliveries.

body.title: What the decade destroyed, and what it built

columns.label: Destroyed
points: The savings of investors who bought at the 1992 and 2000 peaks
Money raised by hundreds of vanishing companies
Trust in the idea that a government-backed fund like US-64 could not fail
Several brokers, a cooperative bank, and many small companies
A generation's willingness to invest in shares, for a while

columns.label: Built
points: A statutory regulator, SEBI, with growing enforcement powers
NSE, screen-based trading and a nationwide market
Access for foreign capital that would power the next boom

body.text: Every boom in this decade had a respectable story: reforms, foreign investors, the internet. Every bust was blamed on a villain: a broker, a promoter, an operator. Both are true, and both miss the point. Scams tend to be exposed at the top of a cycle because rising prices hide them and falling prices reveal them. When a market is euphoric, assume that some of what is rising is being pushed by credit you cannot see.

body.title: Before Applying to an IPO in a Hot Market
steps: Read the risk factors and the use of proceeds in the offer document filed with SEBI, not just the grey market premium on social media
Check whether the business has a record of real profits and cash flow, or only a story
Compare the issue price, as a P/E or price to sales multiple, with listed peers on screener.in
Note how much of the issue is an offer for sale by existing shareholders cashing out, rather than fresh money for the company
Ask whether you would still want the shares if listing day brought no gain at all
Count how many IPOs in the last year are now trading below their issue price

body.title: 2000 and 2021: Same Script?
body.scenario: In late 2021, several Indian new-age technology companies listed amid huge excitement, with high valuations and heavy retail participation. Paytm listed in November 2021 at an issue price of ₹2,150 and fell more than 70% within a year. Zomato, which listed in July 2021 at ₹76, fell sharply in 2022 but then rose to several times its issue price by 2024. A friend says: "This proves every tech IPO is a scam, just like 2000."
body.prompt: Using the tech mania of 1998 to 2001 and the rest of this lesson, what is right and wrong about your friend's conclusion?
body.modelAnswer: Your friend is right that the pattern rhymes. In both 2000 and 2021, a genuine technology shift attracted euphoric demand, companies listed at valuations that assumed years of flawless growth, and many investors bought because of recent gains rather than the business. When the cycle turned, as it did with global rate hikes in 2022, the most richly valued issues fell hardest. But "every tech IPO is a scam" is wrong in two ways. First, a bad investment at a high price is not the same as a fraud: unlike many vanishing companies of the mid 1990s, these were real businesses with disclosed financials, listed under much stronger SEBI rules. Second, outcomes diverged. Just as Infosys and Wipro survived the 2000 bust and went on to create enormous wealth while many K-10 favourites disappeared, Zomato's business improved and its shares recovered strongly, while others did not. The lasting lesson from both eras is the one from Railway Mania: the technology can be real, and the price can still be wrong. Judge each business on its earnings path and valuation, not on the label or the listing-day buzz.

cards.definition: The package introduced after the balance of payments crisis: abolition of most industrial licensing, lower tariffs, openness to foreign investment and, in 1992, free pricing of share issues.
The diversion of bank funds into the stock market through the government securities market, exposed in April 1992. It ended the reform euphoria and strengthened SEBI.
Companies that raised money from the public in the mid 1990s IPO boom and then became untraceable, with promoters disappearing.
Holding shares electronically with a depository such as NSDL or CDSL instead of as paper certificates. Introduced in India from 1996.
A group of shares associated with operator Ketan Parekh during the 1999 to 2000 technology boom, many of which collapsed in 2001.
UTI's July 2001 suspension of repurchases in its flagship US-64 scheme, which had been treated as safe by millions of households. It led to a government rescue and UTI's restructuring.

body.label: SEBI: Public Issue Offer Documents
body.description: SEBI's website publishes draft and final offer documents for public issues under its filings section. Reading the risk factors and objects of the issue is the single best defence against the mistakes of the 1990s IPO boom.

children.text: By April 2003 almost nobody wanted Indian shares. The Sensex was below its 1992 level, retail investors had been burned repeatedly, and the headlines were about scams. That is often what the start of a great cycle looks like. Lesson 3.3 covers the five years that followed, when the Sensex rose roughly seven times.

body.text: Index levels, estimates of scam sizes and other figures in this lesson are approximate and rounded, and sources differ on some details. References to companies and individuals describe widely reported historical events for educational purposes only. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security or investment advice.

points: The 1991 balance of payments crisis triggered reforms that were a genuine displacement: licensing ended, share pricing was freed, SEBI gained statutory powers and FIIs were allowed in

The decade held three booms and busts: reform euphoria ended by the 1992 scam, an FII and IPO boom ended by vanishing companies and external shocks, and a tech mania ended by the 2001 crash and scandal
Both scams of the decade routed bank credit into shares, the same loop seen in the South Sea Bubble and 1860s Bombay
The Sensex fell from about 4,500 in April 1992 to about 2,900 in April 2003, a CAGR of about −3.9% before dividends
The wreckage built the modern market: NSE and screen trading in 1994, dematerialised shares from 1996, derivatives in 2000, and rolling settlement
Scams tend to surface at cycle tops, so treat euphoric markets as places where hidden leverage is likely
A real technology and a good investment are different things, a lesson repeated in 2000 and again with the new-age IPOs of 2021
